internal_silent.note: `ERROR` and `MISSING` are here for the same reason markdown has them: they are tree-sitter's UNIVERSAL parse-failure node types, not python constructs. The grammar emits them wherever a file does not parse, which makes them the parser's error channel rather than a member of the language, and an analyzer correctly derives no symbol from one. They were missing here, and the cost was concrete rather than cosmetic: section A reported "2 node type(s) in NO bucket: ERROR, MISSING", which is a FAIL, and section A is the first of the eight sections a language must pass to reach CONFORMANT. A lane can therefore be blocked from admission by two node types that belong to no language at all — and the diagnostic pointed at the classification rather than at the census, so the fix belongs in the classification.

decisions.node_type: method_signature / method_declaration / function_definition / def / sub (override resolution)
decisions.question: AnalyzeContext.overrideCompanion is never populated by production callers — what must analyzers that gate ALL override emission on it do for externally-declared bases?
decisions.resolution: M37.10 ruling (family-wide): the companion is optional enrichment, never a hard gate. Contract: in-file base declaring the method -> verified override (0.95 php/ruby/python/js/perl, 1.0 java/swift Pass-1); companion present -> companion-index resolution (0.85-0.9); otherwise deterministic Pass-3 first-parent guess at 0.5 with reasonCode 'first-parent-guess' and evidence tier 'inferred' — below the patterns.ts 0.7 threshold, counted as heuristic (honest suspicion) by the F5 differential. Gating on the companion alone silently dropped every cross-file override (php, ruby, python, javascript, perl); the inverse overclaim (swift guess at 1.0/structural) is equally a defect. Gated by F9-PROBE-M3710-* probes, per-language external-override fixtures + confidence pins, and 6 regression mutants.

decisions.node_type: class_definition / argument_list (the base list)
decisions.question: `implements` — does python have a conformance relation DISTINCT from inheritance, so the type is a GAP rather than a ruling?
decisions.resolution: REVERSED 2026-10-09 (PY-27 → PY-34), and the reversal is kept on the record because the earlier verdict was confidently wrong in both directions. WHAT IT USED TO SAY, and why it was wrong: it read `implements` as a SECOND relation that would duplicate 71 `extends` edges, because `issubclass(C, X)` is True for a concrete base, an `abc.ABC` and a `typing.Protocol` alike and X is in `C.__mro__` in all three. Instrument A's measurement is true and was the wrong test: the pinned grammar produces 196 distinct node types and 0 of the 17 conformance-clause names among them, but in python the relation does not arrive as its own node — it arrives INSIDE the base list (`class C(Mapping)`), which is where every other OO language puts `extends`. Instrument B had already counted the construct as present: 71 interface-declaring base entries (14 ABC + 57 Protocol over 16,377 base-list entries, 0.43%). THE RULED ANSWER IS NOW ONE EDGE PER BASE, the most specific true label — `implements` for a PROVEN interface base, `extends` otherwise — with the inheritance fact carried where the store WALKS it: `metadata.superTypes` published from the FULL base list, copied by the indexer into `brain_symbol.super_types`, and read by `member-owner-resolution` and `override-retarget`. The additive reading (both labels for one base) is pinned as a FORBID row by validation/m14/fixtures/python/interface-implements.expectation.json and interface-qualified-subscript-head.expectation.json. WHAT MAKES A BASE PROVEN is the FILE'S OWN IMPORT, never the spelling (`ABC` and `Protocol` are legal user class names; 24 `Protocol` base occurrences live inside CPython's own typing.py), plus the in-file interface base (transitive through headers only), plus one non-inheritance tier: `SomeABC.register(SomeConcrete)` with a PROVEN receiver — measured at 493 `X.register(Y)` calls in 5,984 files and exactly ONE provable receiver (`collections.abc.Sequence.register(Row)`, sqlite3/dbapi2.py:54, in the UNPINNED cpython-stdlib), which is why the pinned-population probe reads 0. MEASURED AFTER: 333 `implements` edges in 97 files over the arbiter's 11,488-file population, 0 UNRESOLVED (201 resolved, 104 external, 25 ambiguous, 3 virtual-registration). Instruments: validation/m14/fixtures/python/implements-probe.ts (calibrated: `--self-test` asserts exact counts, and a corpus run exits non-zero if calibration fails), validation/m14/fixtures/python/oracle-interface-tiers.ts (the ORACLE held against all five interface fixtures' expect/forbid rows, both directions), and script/m14/python-ruled.ts (whose header records the reversal).

decisions.node_type: type (annotations, return annotations, isinstance arguments) — the declared-type reference graph
decisions.question: references to an INTERPRETER BUILTIN (`-> dict`, `-> Exception`, `-> type`) — is a builtin name a legitimate reference target, or a defect? `python-endpoint-defects.ts` class D2 counted 7,687 of them as defects.
decisions.resolution: DECIDED 2026-10-10 (round 3), closing D2 as a DECLARED POSITION rather than a fault. THE RULE: `references` targets are filtered by POSITION and by the 11 SCALARS, not by 'is a builtin'. Of the names written in a type position only `str int float complex bool bytes object None Any self cls` are dropped — they carry no resolution and appear in nearly every file — and EVERY other name is the type the code NAMES, interpreter builtin or not. WHY POSITION IS THE AXIS, measured rather than argued: a synthetic source containing every candidate position emits exactly one `references` edge from a return annotation (`-> Exception`), a typed attribute (`slot: Exception`) and an isinstance check, and NONE from `except Exception as ex:` or `raise ValueError("x")` — so the 180 `BaseException` + 97 `Exception` + 383 `type` edges D2 named are annotation and isinstance facts, not control-flow noise. `python/type-usage-graph` had already pinned the container half of this position (dict/list EXPECT, str/None FORBID) before this session; `python/builtin-type-name-is-still-a-reference` now asserts the four firing rows and `python/builtin-type-name-is-not-a-control-flow-edge` FORBIDS both exception rows, so the rule is falsifiable in BOTH directions (python fixtures 37/37). WHAT REMAINS A DEFECT, AND ITS MEASUREMENT: **D2b** — the same reference arriving from a position that is not `declared_type`/`return_type`/`instanceof_check` — measured at **0 of the 7,687** over the arbiter's 11,488-file population (`npx tsx script/m14/python-endpoint-defects.ts --workers 4`, against D1 0, D3 0, D5 750, D6a 0, D6b 0, D7 0). D2's number is therefore a POPULATION SIZE with a named cause, not a fault count. TO OVERTURN: find a builtin reference emitted from a position outside the three, or a declared position that stops emitting.

decisions.node_type: member position (`calls`/`uses`) — the RELATION-LEVEL OWNER CHANNEL (metadata.owner)
decisions.question: python published NO relation-level `owner` on any member edge (measured: 0 of the whole admitted corpus), so every `calls`/`uses` row whose target is a member name fell to the store's name-keyed ranking — same-file-first, then lexicographic `s.id` as TEXT — which binds `render` to whichever same-named declaration sorts first. That ranking is a tie-break, not a fact about python. Does this lane need the owner channel php's PHPD42 built, and how wide can its boundary safely be?
decisions.resolution: DECIDED 2026-10-10 (round 4). SHIPPED: `real-python-analyzer.ts` now publishes `metadata.owner` on a member-position edge when the receiver is EXACTLY the implicit first parameter, spelled `self` or `cls`, with a single dot (`memberOwnerOf`). That is the same spelling the `dispatch-on-parameter` reason code already trusts, and it is the case the store's rule 0 answers by IDENTITY (the source method's own class), never by a name that could collide. The store's `resolveMemberTargetsByOwner` (`src/ast/member-owner-resolution.ts`) is language-agnostic and scoped by the DATA (the presence of the key), so this activates php's lever for this lane without a language switch. BOUNDARY, and it is load-bearing rather than tidy: `self.store.save` (two dots) carries NO owner, because `save` belongs to the VALUE of `self.store`, whose type nothing in the parse states — labelling it with the ENCLOSING class would let the store bind `save` to a method of the outer class, a confident wrong edge, which is exactly the failure the channel exists to remove; a local receiver (`other.save`) and a module-level `def f(self)` carry none for the same reason. EVIDENCE: `python/member-owner-channel` pins the analyzer signal (three positive rows, two `meta.owner: null` negatives, one forbid); `python/owner-resolution-gate.mts` measures the store pass in isolation with three controls (as-is / no-owner / no-super_types) and pins persistence-by-identity for a colliding class name; `store-heritage-seam.mts` section D measures it through the REAL pipeline (`indexProjectParallel`), including a CROSS-FILE ancestor walk (`UserRepo.read_all -> self.record` resolving to `Repository` in another file); `python/owner-channel-census.mts` prices the lever on a real repo — `requests`: 375 owner-carrying rows of 3,325 member rows (11.3%), 195 RESOLVED (188 direct + 7 inherited), 180 DECLINED. THE DECLINED SPLIT IS DECLARED, NOT HIDDEN: 162 of the 180 are rows where the owner's own class declares the target name TWICE — an attribute declared both as a class-body annotation (`x: T`, PEP 526) and as an instance assignment (`self.x = ...`) is two `contains` edges and two members, which the independent oracle deliberately corroborates (`walkClassBody` and `instanceAttrSeen` in `oracles/python-truth.ts`), and the pass refuses to pick between two genuine declarations rather than guess, the same rule php's gate states. CLOSED 2026-10-10 (round 5), by widening the SHARED pass on a rule about the CANDIDATES rather than about a language: when every candidate shares the owner's identity, the member NAME and the KIND, they are one member published more than once, so the pass resolves to the smallest id instead of declining — while a set with more than one KIND still declines, because a name a class carries as both a method and a property is two DIFFERENT members. The rule is not a tie-break: unlike `ambiguousInChain`, where the choice is between different declarations, these candidates are the same member, so binding to any of them lands the edge on the same node. PHP-NEUTRALITY IS PROVEN, NOT ARGUED: on php's 600-file whole-population sample the new branch fires ZERO times (`sameKindDuplicateResolved=0`), the owner-resolved count is unchanged at 3,354, `ambiguousInChain` is unchanged at 152, and BOTH php's owner-resolution gate and its store-resolution census still PASS. Python's `requests` sample sees it fire 162 times, lifting the owner channel from **195/375 (52.0%)** to **357/375 (95.2%)** resolved — the declines fall to 18 (14 where the class declares no such member, 4 genuinely multi-kind). The `python/owner-resolution-gate.mts` DUPLICATE row (a class declaring `value: int` AND `self.value = 0`) pins the resolution and the counter, and the fixture carries no change because the analyzer is untouched.

decisions.node_type: type (annotations, return annotations, isinstance arguments) — a CALL inside a type expression and its keyword-argument names
decisions.question: In `read_token: Annotated[str, Field(min_length=1, strict=True, max_length=2048)]` the annotation expression holds a CALL. The walk that derives `references` recursed into it and published an edge for every identifier it reached — including `min_length`, `strict`, `max_length`, which are keyword-argument NAMES. Is a keyword-argument name a type reference?
decisions.resolution: NO, and the edge was a FABRICATION: `references Model -> min_length` asserts the class references a type called `min_length`, which names nothing and binds to nothing. FIXED 2026-10-10 (round 6) by making `collectTypeNodes` treat a `keyword_argument` node the way it is treated everywhere else — the NAME child is a parameter label, the VALUE is the expression — so the walk recurses into the value and skips the name. The callee (`Field`) and the subscript head (`Annotated`) are still published, because those ARE names the annotation mentions. THE ORACLE CARRIED THE SAME RECURSION, which is why the differential read green while both sides were wrong; the fix landed in `oracles/python-truth.ts` in the same change, and the differential stayed 100% covered / MISSING 0 / unexplained 0 for both cython and requests. MEASURED: `references` fell from 63,498 to 62,064 edges (\u22121,434 fabricated rows) over the arbiter's 11,488-file population, with the arbiter still `emitted 10/10, FALSIFIED 0`. Pinned by `python/references-do-not-name-keyword-arguments` (two positive rows, five forbids) and by a mutant (`references/keyword-argument-name-is-not-a-type`) that reverts the skip and is CAUGHT. Not every removed edge was a project-unresolved target (many keyword names coincidentally matched a declaration elsewhere), so the verdict's UNEXPLAINED count moved only 6,405 \u2192 6,283 — the edge count is the size of the fabrication, the verdict is the size of the dangling residue.

decisions.node_type: member/target position — the PER-LABEL RESOLUTION VERDICT (all ten labels, incoming AND outgoing)
decisions.question: The lane's earlier work measured whether each type FIRES (arbiter: 10/10) and closed `implements` resolution to zero UNRESOLVED. What is the resolution status of EVERY label, in BOTH directions, and is every unresolved incoming target explained?
decisions.resolution: MEASURED 2026-10-10 (round 6) by `script/m14/python-endpoint-resolution.ts`, which now decomposes each of the ten labels' UNRESOLVED incoming targets by CAUSE — `declared-dynamic` (the edge's own reasonCode says the target is chosen at runtime), `declared-external` (`external-member-call`, reachable through the file's import edge), `qualified-external` (the endpoint's dotted route is rooted at an imported module), `builtin` (the name is one the interpreter owns) — with the fifth axis `UNEXPLAINED` being the ONLY one that names a defect. THE VERDICT over the arbiter's 11,488-file population (205,928 symbols, 1,290,877 relationships): OUTGOING (source) UNRESOLVED is **0 for all ten labels** — no edge lies about WHAT made it; INCOMING UNEXPLAINED is **6,283**, and every other unresolved target is on one of the four explained axes. The residual is DECLARED, not hidden, and each class has a NAMED cause: `calls` 4,837 (a call to a name bound in the ENCLOSING FUNCTION — a nested `def`, a parameter such as pytest's injected fixtures, or a local; the lane publishes no symbol for a local, so the target is a local binding the project-wide index cannot hold — the next lever is a distinct `local-callee` reasonCode); `references` 1,332 and `extends` 105 (names reached through an ALIASED namespace import, `import typing as t` — see PY-D13); `exports` 9 (`__all__` names provided lazily by a module `__getattr__`). PINNED by `validation/m14/fixtures/python/resolution-verdict-gate.ts`, a fast gate over the committed artefact `resolution-verdict.current.json` that FAILS if any label stops emitting, if any label's outgoing UNRESOLVED rises above 0, or if any label's incoming UNEXPLAINED rises above its declared ceiling — so the numbers a doc quotes cannot drift unwatched.

decisions.node_type: import surface — the BOUND NAME of an aliased import (`import X as Y`, `from X import Z as W`)
decisions.question: A file that writes `import typing as t` and then `class C(t.Protocol)` binds the name `t`. Does the import surface publish that binding, so a consumer can resolve `t.Protocol`?
decisions.resolution: ROUND 7 (2026-10-10) — THE LANE-SIDE HALF IS FIXED; THE STORE-SIDE HALF STAYS DECLARED. The analyzer parsed the alias all along (`ImportInfo.alias` for `import X as Y`) and published it on NO relation, so no consumer could see it; `from X import Z as W` was lossy one layer deeper, recording only the imported name in `items` and never the bound `W`. Both shapes now publish the BOUND name on the `imports` edge as `metadata.importedAs` — only when the binding DIFFERS from the imported name, because a key that merely repeats it is noise a consumer has to filter — pinned in both directions by `validation/m14/fixtures/python/import-alias-is-published-as-a-binding.{py,expectation.json}`. MEASURED EFFECT: an independent CPython-`ast` classification of the round-6 verdict's dumped edges found **1,035 of the 1,446** `references`+`extends` UNEXPLAINED rows have their leaf, or their dotted route's root, bound by an `as` import (`t.Callable`, `t.Self`, `t.Protocol`, `nn.Module`); the resolution verdict now reads `metadata.importedAs` off the edge and classifies those routes as `qualified-external` instead of counting them as defects. WHAT REMAINS OPEN, AND WHY IT IS NOT TAKEN HERE: `src/ast/pool-worker.ts`'s `parseFile` projection emits `{name, path, type, isExternal, line}` and drops `alias`, and `src/ast/parallel-indexer.ts` reads `imp.alias ?? imp.localName` — so `brain_import.imported_as` is still NULL for this shape, and the namespace classification is still lost one layer up (`type: "namespace"` is what the projection writes, while the indexer reads `imp.importType`/`imp.isNamespace`). That surface is SHARED and master-owned (every language's stored imports move with it), so it is declared with its measurement rather than changed inside a python round; the lane-side publication is what makes the finding checkable in the meantime.

decisions.node_type: calls — a BARE-NAME callee bound in an ENCLOSING FUNCTION's scope (`local-callee`)
decisions.question: The round-6 verdict left 4,837 `calls` edges whose callee binds to nothing the project declares — the lane's largest UNEXPLAINED class. Is that one defect, many defects, or a fact about the language?
decisions.resolution: ONE FACT, MEASURED INDEPENDENTLY. Reading the top names showed the cause before any code changed: `run_eval` is a NESTED `def` inside `main`, `django_capture_on_commit_callbacks` is a pytest-INJECTED PARAMETER — and both are the same shape: the callee is bound in an ENCLOSING FUNCTION's scope, and this lane publishes no symbol for a local (the JS-family contract: locals, params and lambda params are not symbols). Python's LEGB rule makes that a statement about the language rather than a guess: a name bound in an enclosing function resolves to THAT binding, and a module-level name of the same spelling is shadowed for the whole body — so `local-callee` is the MORE correct answer, not a fallback for a failed lookup. INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENT (CPython `ast`, not the analyzer): over the round-6 verdict's dumped unexplained edges, **4,230 of the 4,837** are calls whose callee IS bound in an enclosing function scope; the residual **607** is NOT that shape — it is `from X import *` (wildcard imports: `test_dataclasses.py` deliberately writes `from dataclasses import *`, `data-types.py` writes `from pyspark.sql.types import *`, and a star import binds every public name of a module, which no per-name static answer can bound) plus two corpus files CPython refuses to parse at all (a test file with deliberately invalid syntax, and an ASN.1 spec file named `.py`), where the analyzer's TREE-based pre-pass still answers. IMPLEMENTATION: a pre-pass (`collectFunctionLocals`) records each function's OWN bindings — parameters, nested `def`/`class` NAMES, and assignment / for-target / `with as` / `except as` / walrus TARGET names — keyed by the function's START POSITION, because a `Node` can never be a key: web-tree-sitter hands back a fresh wrapper on every `.parent`/`.namedChild()` access, so the first version of this map (keyed on the node) hit nothing and every call read `bare-name-callee` — which the probe showed immediately, since the reasons were all one value. The call site asks by walking the CALLEE LEAF's own ancestors, so the answer is lexical and needs no scope bookkeeping, and the nested `def` the main walk deliberately does not open a scope for needs no special case. DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED, each for a reason: a nested function's BODY (its bindings are its own — walking in would mark a call in `outer` to a name bound only in `inner` as local, the over-claim direction); lambda and comprehension targets (their own scopes); `attribute`/`subscript` targets (they bind a member or an element, not a bare name); a parameter's DEFAULT or ANNOTATION expression (only the parameter's `name` field is read, so `def f(x=SOME_DEFAULT)` does not make `SOME_DEFAULT` local); and any name a `global`/`nonlocal` statement declares, which is SUBTRACTED because a write to it targets another scope — the one shape where a naive collector over-claims. The verdict gained the matching `declared-local` axis. PINNED by `validation/m14/fixtures/python/local-callee-is-a-binding-not-a-guess.{py,expectation.json}`, whose forbid rows are the defect direction (a module-level `def` must stay resolvable; a `global`-declared name is not local; a name bound only in a nested function is not local to the outer one) and which six mutants in `script/m14/python-implements-mutants.py` must fail. NOT CLAIMED: that the residual 607 is the lane's defect (it is an unbounded wildcard import or a file CPython cannot parse), nor that these edges RESOLVE — they are the honest 'no project declaration exists' answer, which is a different statement from a resolved edge.

decisions.node_type: references / extends — a TYPE-HOLDING name bound in the ENCLOSING FUNCTION (`local-binding-target`)
decisions.question: After PY-D14 closed the `calls` axis, the verdict's residual histogram showed the SAME fact unlabelled on two other axes: 232 of 389 UNEXPLAINED `references` targets and 14 of 15 UNEXPLAINED `extends` targets. Is the honest answer a label, a resolution, or nothing at all?
decisions.resolution: A LABEL, on the two axes that lack one, and the population was priced BEFORE the code changed. INDEPENDENT MEASUREMENT (CPython `ast` over the verdict's dumped edge list — the interpreter's parser, not this analyzer's tree): of the 389 `references` targets, **232** name a binding of an enclosing function, **52** are PEP-695 type parameters (PY-D16), **64** are in files CPython cannot parse at all (ASN.1 specifications named `.py`; named here, not fixed here), **26** are `from X import *` bindings (`test_dataclasses.py` writes `from dataclasses import *`, so `InitVar`/`KW_ONLY` are outside any per-name answer), **12** are the RECEIVER prefix of a dotted annotation naming a module handle produced by a call (`helloworld_pb2, helloworld_pb2_grpc = grpc.protos_and_services(...)` — the head identifier the annotation walk publishes deliberately, per `qualified-endpoint-spellings`), and **3** are a member read of a receiver whose type is unknown (`self._self_owner` inside `isinstance(instance, self._self_owner)`). Of the 15 `extends` targets, **14** are a dynamic BASE (`class Row(dump_cls)` where `dump_cls = _py_row.BaseRow` or `_cy_row.BaseRow` was chosen by an `if`; `class Sub(TemplateIter)` where `TemplateIter = type(iter(t''))`) and 1 is in a CPython-unparseable file. WHY A LABEL AND NOT A RESOLUTION: the position code the lane already published (`instanceof-check`) is TRUE and useless — `isinstance(obj, type_or_tuple)` where `type_or_tuple` is a WALRUS TARGET of the same condition is a dict lookup at runtime, and a consumer cannot tell it from `isinstance(instance, SomeClass)`. The position is not lost (it stays in `metadata.relationshipType`, whose whole job that is); `reasonCode` NARROWS to the binding whenever the binding is what blocks resolution, which is what M14 §4 asks a reason code to say. IMPLEMENTATION: `dynamicTypeBindingReason(leaf, name, locals)` walks the target leaf's ANCESTORS and answers from the pre-pass `collectFunctionLocals` (PY-D14) — the same lexical-position property that makes `isLocalCalleeName` correct for a nested def three levels up — and it is a SEPARATE helper rather than a widening of that one, because a call's target is a callee (`local-callee`) and a reference's is a type, and putting one vocabulary on two axes is the mistake `external-member-call`/`dispatch-on-receiver` are deliberately separated to avoid. The `extends` emitter publishes it too, and that axis had NO reason code at all before this round (unfilterable rather than imprecise); confidence stays 1.0 there because the SOURCE fact is exact — the class body's base list is literally those names — which is the same reasoning that already lets `implements` carry a code at 1.0. The verdict's `declared-local` axis now covers three codes (`local-callee`, `local-binding-target`, `inline-type-parameter`): one axis because the fact is the same (LEGB resolves it locally and makes any module-level namesake a shadowed name), three codes because the KIND of binding differs and the codes are what a consumer queries. PINNED by `validation/m14/fixtures/python/reference-binding-is-not-a-guess.{py,expectation.json}` — whose controls are the over-claim direction (a module-level name at the same isinstance position keeps `instanceof-check`; an ordinary module-level base keeps no code) and whose `typed_local` pair pins BOTH readings of ONE local name (`kind: type` keeps `annotation-type`, `isinstance(obj, kind)` one line later carries `local-binding-target`) — and by three mutants in `script/m14/python-implements-mutants.py` (axis removed, claimed for everything, base axis reverted). NOT CLAIMED: that the 64 ASN.1 edges, the 26 wildcard rows, the 12 module-handle receivers or the 3 member reads are defect-free; each is named and counted here, and only the first has an identified mechanism (a `references` edge derived from inside a parse-ERROR subtree — a candidate for its own round, not silently widened into this one).

decisions.node_type: references — a PEP-695 INLINE TYPE PARAMETER (`inline-type-parameter`)
decisions.question: `def first[U](items: list[U]) -> U` references `U` twice, and `U` is declared — by the def's own signature. Should the lane publish a symbol for it, so the edges RESOLVE, or declare it?
decisions.resolution: DECLARE IT, because publishing it is a lie about scope twice over. Python binds a PEP-695 parameter in the def's (or class's) OWN lexical scope; it is reachable nowhere else, so a file-scope symbol would claim accessibility the language does not grant — and the corpus contains the shape that makes the cost concrete: `ansible_test/_internal/cache.py` declares `[TValue]` on BOTH `get` and `get_with_args`, so a symbol-per-parameter rule publishes two symbols of ONE name in one file, which the store can only report as ambiguous and then rank by `id`, i.e. a tie-break presented as a resolution. MEASURED: 52 of the 389 UNEXPLAINED `references` targets (13.4%), identified with CPython's `ast` `type_params` field rather than inferred from bracket syntax, and the names are exactly the TypeVar-shaped ones a reader would misdiagnose (`TValue`, `TIntegrationTarget`, `THostConfig`, `THostProfile`, `TRemoteConfig`, `TCompletionConfig`, `TIntegrationConfig`). This is the one axis where the lane's answer is `declared-local` while the target is a TYPE and not a value, which is why it carries its own code rather than folding into PY-D15's: the fact a consumer needs is that the name IS a type and IS declared, just not where any project-wide declaration can live. IMPLEMENTATION: `typeParameterNames(def)` reads the `type_parameter` clause off the enclosing def/class and takes the FIRST identifier of each parameter, which is the name in every shape the grammar produces — `[TValue]` is `type -> identifier`, the BOUNDED `[T: str]` is `type -> constrained_type -> type -> identifier`, and a splat is a pattern whose first identifier is likewise the name — so a `bound` is never mistaken for a parameter (the mutant that reads the clause from the other end, yielding `int` for `[W: int]`, must fail). The local check runs first, because python's function scope is one namespace: a def that both declares `[T]` and assigns `T = ...` binds a local at runtime, and naming the signature's binding there would be wrong. PINNED by `validation/m14/fixtures/python/inline-type-parameter-is-not-a-class.{py,expectation.json}`, whose central assertion is that `U`, `V` and `W` are NOT symbols while the module-level `TypeVar` `T` IS one — the difference that makes their absence a decision rather than an inability — and whose controls are the module-level TypeVar reference keeping its position code and the bound `int` never becoming a reference. NOT CLAIMED: that PEP-695 parameters are rare in future code, which is the opposite of the trend and the reason the shape was worth a code rather than a comment.

decisions.node_type: references / calls — a clause the parser FLAGGED (`hasError`)
decisions.question: `def f(d: double[:], o: Optional[double[:]])` published `references f -> o` — a PARAMETER claimed to be a type. `double[:]` is VALID CPython (an annotation is an arbitrary expression; `double[:]` is a slice of the name `double`), so the author wrote nothing wrong. Should the lane keep reading the annotation, or refuse it?
decisions.resolution: REFUSE THE WHOLE CLAUSE, because the tree it was read from does not match the source and the names inside it are therefore not a reading. tree-sitter's python grammar rejects a slice used as an annotation, so the parameter list collapses into ONE `typed_parameter` whose `type` clause swallowed `, o: Optional[...]` and presented `o` inside a synthesised `constrained_type`. That is a CONFIDENTLY-WRONG edge, the class the arc puts below an honest NULL, and the same class as PY-D11 (a keyword argument's NAME published as a type) and as the empty-identifier guard this collector already carries. The rule is the parser's own verdict rather than a heuristic about names: a type clause whose subtree contains an error (`hasError`) names no type at all. THE COST IS DECLARED, not hidden: the well-formed-looking `double` and `Optional` inside that same garbled clause are refused WITH it, because a name read out of a structure the parser got wrong is luck, not reading. What is NOT refused is the CLAUSE THAT IS CLEAN IN A FILE THAT ERRORS: `def f(d: double[:]) -> None` keeps `double`, because in its tree the `type` clause is `(type (identifier))` and the ERROR is a SIBLING of it, and a rule that refused every clause in an erroring file would trade a fabrication for a silent loss. MEASURED on the full-population verdict: the guard removes the fabricated rows and the fixture pins both directions. THE SAME RULE ON THE CALL SIDE refuses a call whose own subtree the parser flagged, and a call the parser swallowed into an ERROR node — which is how an ASN.1 document carrying a `.py` extension produced `calls BitStr -> SIZE` and `-> sunday` (`otp/lib/asn1/test/asn1_SUITE_data/*.py`, 22 files). PAIRED CHANGE, PROVEN BY FALSIFICATION: `script/m14/oracles/python-truth.ts` derives the same edges for the differential, and WITHOUT the mirrored guard it derives the same fabricated `references f -> o` — the differential then reads AGREEMENT, the two-derivations-of-one-unstated-assumption trap PY-D11 named. Measured directly by removing the oracle's guard while leaving the analyzer's in place: cython reports `MISSING=1`, and that one missing edge IS the fabrication. Restored, both lanes report `MISSING=0 unexplained=0`. NOTE ON COMPARING DIFFERENTIAL TOTALS ACROSS RUNS: they are NOT comparable — the cold-pool rotation deliberately draws never-sampled files each wave (its own comment: `the rotation counter ... reproducible, but every wave sees fresh files`), so a change in `tree-truth` between two runs is a change of FILE SET, not an effect. Only the within-run relationship (covered/MISSING/unexplained) and the result hash mean anything across runs. PINNED by `validation/m14/fixtures/python/parser-error-region-is-not-a-type.{py,expectation.json}`: forbid `f -> o` (the fabrication), forbid `f -> double` and `f -> Optional` (the declared cost, so a later round cannot narrow the guard to just the embarrassing identifier), and KEEP `clean_subscript -> Optional`/`-> list`, `clean_union -> Mapping`/`-> dict` and `slice_alone_keeps_its_type -> double` (the over-correction direction). Mutants: `parser-error/type-clause-claims-again` (revert), `parser-error/no-clause-is-trusted` (the over-correction) and `parser-error/call-in-error-region` (the call side).

decisions.node_type: calls / references — a name bound by `global X` plus a CREATING write in one function
decisions.question:
`global X` in a function plus a write to X in that same function body binds X in the MODULE namespace (CPython: `exec("def f():
 global X
 X=1
f()")` leaves X in `globals()`), yet no module-scope declaration exists unless the module ALSO assigns X at top level — and the pre-pass deliberately SUBTRACTS a `global`-declared name from the function's local set, so the name is neither local nor declared. 98 rows of the round-9 residual hang on exactly this shape (8 calls, 90 references; every call `bare-name-callee`, every reference `annotation-type`). Is the honest output an excuse (a reason code saying the route is unknowable) or a declaration?
decisions.resolution: A DECLARATION, not an excuse — python names the scope and the scope is this file. `publishGlobalWriteBindings` emits an OWNERLESS module-scope Variable for each name a function's own body creates through `global`, at the line of the earliest creating write, marked `isModuleVariable` + `boundByGlobalWrite`. The resolver then finds it by name like any other declaration, so the edge RESOLVES instead of being excused: an excuse would be weaker than the source allows. PRICED BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN, with CPython's own `ast` (`.tmp-py/price-globals9.py`): 397 `global`+creating-write pairs in the corpus, 140 with a module-level binding already (so not this mechanism's), 257 matter pairs, 98 rows on the round-9 residual dump — and it was priced against the OTHER mechanisms too (9 pairs are RMW/del-only and are NOT claimed; 78 are `nonlocal`, a different scope, and are NOT claimed; overlap with the wildcard mechanism is ZERO). PRECISION, re-measured against CPython rather than taken from the price: a creating write needs a VALUE (`exec("x: int", m.__dict__)` adds no namespace entry, so a valueless annotation does NOT create — the price script counted it and the implementation must not); `X += 1` requires the binding to exist and `del X` removes it, so `augmented_assignment` and `delete_statement` do not count; OWN BODY ONLY, because a nested `def`/`class` has its own `global` statements (each nested function is visited as its own node, so an outer `global` plus an inner write is NOT a pair — CPython makes the inner assignment a local). THE DEDUPE IS HALF THE RULE: a name already declared at module scope, or bound by an import, gets NO second declaration (the import case is the conservative direction — one alias per ImportInfo row cannot be split per item). EVIDENCE: `validation/m14/fixtures/python/global-write-creates-module-binding.{py,expectation.json}` (positive: RUN/INNER_ONLY/P; precision: ANNOT_ONLY/COUNTER/GONE/NOT_A_PAIR all 0 symbols; dedupe: BOUND exactly 1, os 0); `script/m14/python-implements-mutants.py` (37/37 CAUGHT, incl. the four round-10 mutants that re-open the disabled symbol, the valueless-annotation read, the nested-body read and the dropped dedupe); the fresh verdict's UNEXPLAINED drop on `calls` and `references` (numbers in the round-10 doc section and in the verdict gate's cause texts).

decisions.node_type: imports — `from M import *`, and the bare names it can bind
decisions.question: `from M import *` binds M's public namespace into THIS module, so a bare name in such a file has a binding route that lives in M. Two facts make the shape invisible: the analyzer spells BOTH `from M import *` and `import M` as the target `M:*`, and the store's per-item projection (`pool-worker`: `{name, path, type, isExternal, line}`) flattens both to `{name: "*", type: "namespace"}` — a two-way loss, so nothing below the analyzer can tell a wildcard from a module handle. 171 rows of the round-9 residual (163 calls, 8 references) sit in files whose every star module is out of view. Should those rows be declared external, resolved, or left as defects?
decisions.resolution: DECLARED, with a gate — and the fact gets a home first. The analyzer publishes `metadata.starImport: true` on its OWN `imports` edge for the wildcard spelling (the same doctrine as PY-D13's `metadata.importedAs`: a fact the projection cannot carry is stated on the surface the verdict reads), and the verdict gains an axis, `star-import-external`, placed after `qualified-external` and before `builtin`. THE GATE IS THE WHOLE HONESTY: the excuse is handed out only when EVERY module the file star-imports is OUT OF VIEW, because an IN-VIEW star module is CHECKABLE (the row being residual already proves that module's public namespace does not declare the name) and a relative star (`from . import *`) is this project by construction. Only BARE names are eligible — `a.b` and `M:item` are other spellings. The decision lives in `script/m14/python-star-axis.ts` rather than inside the census, because an 11,488-file script cannot be falsified without running one: `validation/m14/fixtures/python/star-import-axis-gate.mts` exercises all nine directions (out-of-view excused; in-view by leaf, by dotted path and by module scope all blocked; relative blocked; unnamed blocked; dotted target blocked; `module:item` blocked; no stars blocked). PRICED with CPython (`.tmp-py/price-star-round9.py`): 171 rows whose every star module is out of view, 0 rows blocked by the in-view gate, zero overlap with PY-D18's population. WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED: no symbol is invented for a wildcard-bound name (`make_dataclass` stays a bare-name call with 0 symbols, pinned by the fixture) — the declaration is about the ROUTE being external, not about a resolution nothing can check. EVIDENCE: `validation/m14/fixtures/python/star-import-is-a-binding-rule.{py,expectation.json}`; `validation/m14/fixtures/python/star-import-axis-gate.mts`; `script/m14/python-implements-mutants.py` (round10/star-import-fact-dropped CAUGHT); the verdict's new axis counts per label in `resolution-verdict.current.json`.

decisions.node_type: assignment \u2014 a MULTI-TARGET assignment (`a, b = f()`, `(a, (b, c)) = f()`, `[a, b] = f()`, `a, *rest = f()`)
decisions.question: `extractAssignment` gated on `left.type === "identifier"` and returned for every other target shape, so a multi-target assignment published NOTHING at module scope and nothing at class scope. The names it binds are real bindings of the scope the statement is written in (CPython: `a, b = f()` puts both in `globals()` at module level and both in `vars(C)` in a class body), so the graph carried edges to names the file itself binds. 12 rows of the round-10 UNEXPLAINED dump are exactly this shape (11 references to `helloworld_pb2` + 1 to `helloworld_pb2_grpc` in `pb-grpc`'s examples, all bound by `helloworld_pb2, helloworld_pb2_grpc = grpc.protos_and_services("helloworld.proto")`). Is the honest output a declaration per bound name, or an excuse?
decisions.resolution: A DECLARATION PER BOUND NAME \u2014 the source names the scope and the names, and both halves are checkable. The target is read with the SHARED pattern walker (`patternTargetNodes`, the node-returning face of round 10's `addPatternTargets`), so this reader and PY-D14's local collector cannot disagree about what a binding target is \u2014 the defect class that survived nine rounds in `collectFunctionLocals`'s `with_item` case. The module body publishes one ownerless Variable per name at the name's OWN position, the class body one Property per name with the class as owner, each carrying `metadata.multiTargetForm` (the spelling that bound it: `pattern_list` / `tuple_pattern` / `list_pattern`) \u2014 provenance rather than meaning, the same job `boundByGlobalWrite` does for PY-D18. PRICED BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN with CPython's own `ast` over the verdict's population (`.tmp-py/price-tuple-targets.py`, repo-prefixed keys fixed and the 1 MiB bound applied): 182 module-scope tuple-target names in 58 files, 15 class-body names, 28,136 function-body names \u2014 and the blast on the round-10 residual is 12 rows, all references. THE WALKER GAINED ONE LITERAL AND THE REASON IS MEASURED: `a, *rest = f()` spells the splat as a `list_splat_pattern` element holding one identifier, which the walker did not descend, so `rest` bound nothing at module scope AND was not a function local either (`.tmp-py/round11-shapes.mts` pins the grammar shape; the fixture pins the name). SCOPE IS THE OTHER HALF AND IT IS PINNED IN THE NEGATIVE DIRECTION: a tuple target inside a `def` binds LOCALS, which are not symbols on this family's contract, so `m`/`n`/`sb`/`tail` must count ZERO and their call reads `local-callee` \u2014 the fix publishes declarations only where python binds them. EVIDENCE: `validation/m14/fixtures/python/multi-target-assignment-binds-names.{py,expectation.json}` (eight symbol rows incl. the splat and the chained form, three relationship rows, seven symbol-count rows that are all zero for the locals); six round-11 mutants incl. the disabled target walker, the dropped splat literal, the dropped provenance field and the restored round-10 gate.

decisions.node_type: calls / references \u2014 a read of a comprehension's own `for` target, or of a lambda's own parameter
decisions.question: `collectFunctionLocals` SKIPS comprehension and lambda nodes on purpose and says so: "a lambda's or a comprehension's own parameters are not collected, so a call inside one stays `bare-name-callee` and is counted, never mislabelled". The skip is right about SCOPE and wrong about the CONSEQUENCE: `isLocalCalleeName` and `dynamicTypeBindingReason` then find no enclosing scope that binds the name, so they publish `bare-name-callee` / `annotation-type` \u2014 a claim that the name is a PROJECT-WIDE name \u2014 for a name the source binds in the same expression (`[comp(page) for comp in comparison]`). 11 rows of the round-10 residual are this shape. Is the claim wrong, or is the under-claim safe?
decisions.resolution: THE CLAIM WAS WRONG, and the under-claim was only cheaper. A comprehension's `for` target and a lambda's parameter are bindings of their OWN scope, so a read of one inside that scope is a LOCAL read by python's scoping rules \u2014 `local-callee` for a call, `local-binding-target` for a reference. The fix is `scopeOwnBindings(scope)`: the SAME ancestor walk the function check already performs, asked at each scope node for its OWN bindings, so no state is threaded and no scope bookkeeping is introduced. MEASURED SHAPES (`.tmp-py/round11-shapes.mts`): a comprehension's clauses are all DIRECT children (`for_in_clause`, `left` = identifier or `pattern_list` \u2014 read through the shared pattern walker, so `for k, v in ...` binds two names), and a lambda's parameters live under `lambda_parameters`, a spelling different from a `def`'s `parameters`, which is why the parameter reader was extracted as `addParameterNames` and shared rather than copied. THE PRECISION IS THE LEVER'S WHOLE HONESTY, and it is LEXICAL rather than name-keyed: the same name read AFTER the comprehension is not bound by it (python 3 gives a comprehension its own scope), and a name the comprehension does not bind is not bound at all \u2014 both stay `bare-name-callee`, and both are pinned by the fixture (one of them reads the SAME name as the positive row, one function above it), because the cheap wrong fix \u2014 adding comprehension targets to the enclosing FUNCTION's local set \u2014 passes every positive row and fails exactly those two. The helper's `locals.size === 0` early exit also went: it made the answer `false` for a whole module-scope comprehension in a file with no `def`, which the fixture pins with a module-level comprehension. PRICED with CPython (`.tmp-py/price-comprehension-targets.py`): 13,247 comprehensions and 3,348 lambda scopes, 24,578 such reads in 2,621 files, 11 rows on the round-10 residual (10 calls + 1 reference) with ZERO on the lambda side \u2014 the lambda case is fixed because it is the same fact with a different spelling, and the price says so rather than a corpus row. EVIDENCE: `validation/m14/fixtures/python/comprehension-target-is-a-local.{py,expectation.json}` (five positive rows incl. a second clause and a module-scope comprehension, two precision rows, five zero symbol counts); five round-11 mutants incl. each reader dropped, the lambda case dropped, the first-clause-only read and the cheap wrong fix.

decisions.node_type: references — an isinstance()/issubclass() TYPE argument written as a MEMBER read
decisions.question: `isinstance(instance, self._self_owner)`, `issubclass(source.__class__, field.related_model)` and `isinstance(w.message, passlib_exc.PasslibHashWarning)` publish the last identifier as the edge TARGET with the full spelling in `metadata.qualified`. A member read on a receiver whose root is a LOCAL of an enclosing function has NO static target, so the code is `member-read` — a reason the lane already declares (the `uses` emitter has published it for member reads since before this round). The gate is the receiver's ROOT through python's own lexical walk, which keeps the rule narrow in both directions: an import-bound root (`os.PathLike`) keeps `instanceof-check` and the verdict's `qualified-external` route (893 rows depend on it), and a class this file declares keeps the chance to resolve against the store. Two measured negatives are pinned as rows AND as a mutant: the RECEIVER leaf itself must keep `local-binding-target` — the first version of the rule relabelled it, and `.tmp-py/round12-shape-probe.mts` showed three rows of it before the rule shipped — and `metadata.qualified` still carries the whole spelling, so the route is not lost. decisions.node_type: the VERDICT AXIS for a name no binding in the file can supply (`not-bound-in-file`)
decisions.question: After round 11 the residual is 96: 42 rows in files CPython cannot parse, 47 bare names, 7 lazy `__all__` exports. The 47 are UNEXPLAINED, which on this lane's contract means 'the analyzer cannot say WHY'. But 'the file binds nothing of this name, and nothing it imports can supply it' is a complete, checkable statement about a python read — not a mystery. Should the verdict say it?
decisions.resolution: YES, and only behind a measurement. The axis fires when the edge's OWN reasonCode says the analyzer's binding checks found nothing (`bare-name-callee`, or the position codes `annotation-type` / `instanceof-check` that the emitter falls back to when no binding reason is found), the target is UNRESOLVED against every declaration in the population, and the file does not import the leaf. Why the resolution above already exhausted the file's bindings: a module- or class-scope declaration IS in the store (PY-D21 and PY-D23 publish every statement kind that writes one) and would have resolved or gone ambiguous; a local/comprehension/lambda binding would have set a `local-…` code instead. decisions.node_type: a MODULE-level `def __getattr__(name)` (PEP 562) — the names it PROVIDES, and the `exports` edges they let resolve
decisions.question: The verdict's last 7 UNEXPLAINED incoming rows were all `exports`, and TWO of them are `tree_sitter_clean/__init__.py -> HIGHLIGHTS_QUERY` and `-> TAGS_QUERY`. That file states the provision in its own source: a module-level `def __getattr__(name)` with `if name == "HIGHLIGHTS_QUERY": return _get_query(...)`, the same for `TAGS_QUERY`, and BOTH also listed in `__all__`. `hasattr(module, name)` is TRUE for every such name at runtime and `from module import name` succeeds, so the name is public surface — but the analyzer published no declaration for it, so the module's OWN export edge could not resolve against its own file. Is the row a resolution defect, a truth-side defect, or a provision the lane simply never read?
decisions.resolution: THE LANE NEVER READ THE PROVISION, and the provision is written in the file, so it is readable without executing anything. A module-level `__getattr__` is now read for the names it SPELLS: the comparison's left side must be the function's OWN first parameter name (NOT the literal word `name`), the operator must be `==` or `in`, the right side must be a string literal or a tuple/list/SET of them, and the literal's value must be a python identifier. Each name is published as a module Variable at the STRING LITERAL's own line, carrying `metadata.boundByBinder: "getattr"` — the key round 12 introduced for `for`/`with`/`except` binders, with a value naming THIS mechanism, so no new metadata key enters the worker seam and PY-D26's 17-published/1-carried measurement is unchanged. A comparison whose enclosing `if` CONSEQUENTLY raises `AttributeError` is the INVERTED shape: it states what the module REFUSES, so it is skipped rather than published as a declaration. The guard is cheap and unbounded in the other direction, and that asymmetry is the whole argument for having it. PRICED TWICE with CPython's own `ast` over the corpus, BEFORE the rule existed, and the second pass is the authority: the first was written to classify the 7 rows and its literal shape hardcoded the parameter spelling and accepted sets, the second (`.tmp-py/price-module-getattr-round14.py`) measures THIS rule — 26 of 11,245 parsed files define a module-level `__getattr__` (55 rejected by CPython), 6 of them spell literal names while 20 spell none (they forward to `globals()`, build a dict, import dynamically), those 6 hold 14 literal names, 1 is already statically bound in its own file (cython's `gs`) and 2 are already in their file's import channel, so the rule publishes 11 symbols. THE PRICE IS WHAT FOUND TWO BUGS IN THE CODE THIS ROUND WROTE, and both were found by measuring the shipped analyzer rather than by re-reading the rule: (1) an ANNOTATED parameter (`def __getattr__(name: str)` — 6 of the 26 files) parses as `typed_parameter`, and the first version refused any parameter that was not a bare `identifier`, which silently published 6 fewer names; (2) `ansible/module_utils/_text.py` spells one branch `elif importable_name in {"to_bytes", "to_native", "to_text"}` — a SET — and the first version accepted only tuple/list, publishing 3 fewer names, all in that one `elif`. Both are fixed, and both are pinned as mutants. VERIFIED, not asserted: `.tmp-py/census-getattr-provisions.mts` walks exactly the 6 files the price names and reads 11 published, 0 unexplained misses, with `14 - 1 - 2 = 11` as its own last line; the verdict instrument over all 11,488 files reads totalSymbols 206,940 -> 206,951 (exactly +11) and `exports` incoming UNEXPLAINED 7 -> 5, with the two closed rows named and the remaining five named; the gate's declared ceiling moves 7 -> 5 with its cause rewritten to the two mechanisms that remain. FALSIFIED in both directions: the fixture `python/module-getattr-provides-names` pins every spelling the rule reads and the four ways it must refuse, and 9 new mutants (59 total) are CAUGHT with 0 survivors, including the restored annotated-parameter refusal, the restored hardcoded `name` spelling, the restored set refusal, the deny-list publication, the dropped class gate and the dropped module-half per-NAME dedupe. NOT CLAIMED: the fixture is where the runner's EXPORT INVARIANT bit — an `exports` edge whose target is no top-level symbol of the file is a violation, so the fixture was rewritten rather than the check weakened, and the corpus instance of that shape is declared in PY-D30 instead of pinned as correct.

decisions.node_type: `exports` — an `__all__` entry satisfied by a SUBMODULE the package ships (4 of the 5 remaining verdict rows)
decisions.question: `sqlalchemy/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/__init__.py` lists `mssql`, `mysql`, `oracle` and `postgresql` in `__all__`, binds none of them, imports none of them and names none in a `__getattr__` — yet all four are importable, because the package SHIPS `dialects/mssql/__init__.py` and python's import system supplies the attribute. Can the analyzer publish a declaration for a name whose provider is a sibling file?
decisions.resolution: NO, and the boundary is the analyzer's INPUT rather than its rule set: the analyzer is handed ONE FILE's text, so it can see that `__all__` names `mssql` and cannot see that a directory of that name sits beside it. Publishing a declaration anyway would invent a POSITION for a name the file writes nowhere, which is the fabrication the lane's endpoint rules exist to stop — and the row would then read RESOLVED against a symbol whose span is a guess. This is a resolution-layer fact, not a parse fact, and the layer that has the filesystem is the store. Priced so the deferral has a number: 3,043 `__all__` entries corpus-wide reduce to 6 satisfied by a submodule (`.tmp-py/module-getattr-exports-price.json`, `allSubmoduleRows`) of which 4 are in the verdict's population, 1 more is satisfied by a getattr literal (now published, and separately projected out), and 1 by nothing at all (PY-D30). The gate's declared ceiling for `exports` records these 4 by name.

decisions.node_type: `exports` — an `__all__` entry NOTHING in the file supplies (a stale export; 1 of the 5 remaining verdict rows)
decisions.question: `sqlalchemy/lib/sqlalchemy/ext/declarative/__init__.py` lists `instrument_declarative` in `__all__`; the file binds it nowhere, imports it nowhere, ships no submodule of that name and names it in no `__getattr__`. At runtime the module has no such attribute and `from ... import *` would fail on it — the file's own export list is WRONG. Does the analyzer keep the edge it reads from that list, or filter it to the entries the file can supply?
decisions.resolution: THE EDGE STAYS, and the row is declared instead of hidden. `exports` is the statement being read — the file's `__all__` — and a stale entry is a fact about the source: the analyzer reporting it is the analyzer working. Filtering the edge would make the graph agree with a file that disagrees with itself, and it is the one behaviour a consumer would most want flagged rather than silently dropped. What is NOT legitimate is calling the resulting unresolved target unexplained-by-accident, so the residual is declared with its population: 3,043 `__all__` entries corpus-wide, 6 supplied by nothing (`.tmp-py/module-getattr-exports-price.json`, `allUnknownRows`), 1 of them in the verdict's population, and round 12's `not-bound-in-file` axis is deliberately NOT applied to it — for the submodule rows the axis's claim is false by construction (the file does supply the name, through the import system), and for this row the axis's claim is TRUE, which is exactly why it is declared as a stale export rather than excused as an unresolvable one.

decisions.question: The guard that keeps a published binding from shadowing a declaration the file already made read `ctx.imports` FILE-WIDE, so a name bound by a FUNCTION-LOCAL import blocked the publication of a module-scope provision: `cython/Cython/Build/__init__.py`'s `build_ext` (provided by its `__getattr__`, imported locally inside the very branch that provides it) and `ansible/module_utils/_text.py`'s `codecs` (the same shape) were not published. The same situation spelled `from os import sep as X` published `X`, because the channel holds the imported ITEM name and not the bound alias. Round 14 declared the pair rather than narrowing the guard, with the reason stated: the same guard serves round 12's binder rows, and that count's sensitivity to the change was unmeasured.
decisions.resolution: THE GUARD IS NOW SCOPED TO MODULE-SCOPE IMPORTS, and the price is what settled it. `.tmp-py/price-guard-narrowing.py` mirrors the SHIPPED channel construction (`import a.b` contributes its ROOT, `import a.b as c` contributes BOTH, `from m import a, b` contributes the ITEM names and never a bound alias), computes the candidates the walk would publish at module scope (`for`/`with as`/`except as` targets plus the provision names PY-D28 reads) and reads, over 11,245 parsed files: the guard drops EXACTLY 2 candidates corpus-wide (`build_ext`, `codecs`), both provisions and both dropped by a FUNCTION-LOCAL import, while the BINDER half loses ZERO rows. That retires the round-14 worry by measurement rather than by argument: narrowing moves no round-12 number, so there was nothing left to weigh. The walk already knew the answer — it never enters a function body and it sets `currentClass` inside a class body, so any import statement it pops with no class open is module scope by construction, and it records those lines into `moduleScopeImportLines`, which the guard now consults. An import row with no line (never observed; both handlers set `range`) is KEPT, so a missing position cannot silently widen the publication. MEASURED on the whole population, against the committed artefact: `totalSymbols` 206,951 -> 206,953 (+2, exactly the priced names), every edge count unchanged (1,290,653), every label's `unexplained` unchanged (`exports` still 5), and EXACTLY ONE resolution cell moved — `uses` at project scope, RESOLVED 46,922 -> 46,923 and EXTERNAL 155 -> 154, because `codecs` is a name nothing in the corpus declared before and one thing declares now, so a row that had no declaration to bind to has one. The AMBIGUOUS counts did not move anywhere: publishing these 2 names created no second declaration of any spelling already in the corpus, which is the risk this guard exists against and the reason the fixture pins a module-scope-import row as a FORBID. The row that moved is not pinned by name (the verdict's examples are a sample of 6, and pinning one row needs a per-axis dump = another whole-population run); what is pinned is the cell and its direction. FALSIFIABLE both ways: the fixture's `SHADOWED_BY_LOCAL_IMPORT` count went 0 -> 1 and `path` (bound by a MODULE-scope import) stays forbidden, and two mutants are CAUGHT — `round15/guard-reads-file-wide-import-channel` (the round-14 read restored) and `round15/guard-ignores-import-channel-entirely` (the over-correction that drops the check instead of scoping it).
